title: What If You Could Breathe Underwater?

shots.line: Two metres under a lake.
shots.scene: lake: dusk. Wide low over still water, pier on left, camera sinks below the surface; TIMESTACK "Day one / dusk / 2 m down"
shots.footnote: Illustration · hypothetical person · not a real event

shots.line: A pier above, a clay-white shape below. One person. Eyes open. Mouth open.
shots.scene: lake: Underwater clay swimmer drifts from pier post; slow orbit, mouth and eyes open, bubbles absent; tag "ONE PERSON"

shots.line: In the corner of the frame, a stopwatch starts. Ten seconds. Thirty. A minute.
shots.scene: lake: Close on swimmer, stopwatch TIMECHIP counts 0:10, 0:30, 1:00 on the words; camera slow push

shots.line: She is not holding her breath. She is breathing. The water goes in. Something comes out.
shots.scene: lake: Side view of swimmer's face and neck; water streams in at the mouth as a pale ribbon (K.ribbon); no distress

shots.line: Her chest rises and falls like anyone's on dry land. Nobody on the pier knows how. The answer is not in her lungs.
shots.scene: lake: Chest rises and falls, camera on torso; cut to pier above: two clay figures at the edge, empty looking

shots.line: It is in a number.
shots.scene: lake: Dark dip; single white dot grows at frame centre

shots.line: Two hundred and fifty. This is the story of one rule. A person who can breathe water.
shots.scene: card: HERO stat "250" with label "mL of oxygen per minute"; flash in
shots.footnote: Source: resting adult, standard physiology teaching

shots.line: Of a litre of air and a litre of lake. And the gap between them.
shots.scene: bench: clay. Two glass jars on a table, left labelled AIR right LAKE, camera pushes between them

shots.line: Of a fish that solves the problem with a plumbing trick.
shots.scene: gill: studio dark. Trout silhouette turns slowly, gill slit highlighted with ring

shots.line: And a lung that was never built for it.
shots.scene: torso: clay. Lung cutaway, spinning slowly, ring on trachea

shots.line: Of mice in a tank in the nineteen-sixties, and premature babies in a hospital in Philadelphia.
shots.scene: card: Two-panel statement: "1960s · mice in a tank" and "Philadelphia · premature babies"; no pictures of infants

shots.line: And an empty pier at dusk. Could a human really do it?
shots.scene: lake: dusk. Empty pier at dusk, camera drifts along planks; title card "COULD A HUMAN REALLY DO IT?"

shots.line: And what would it cost her, minute by minute?
shots.scene: card: LIST card "And what would it cost her, minute by minute?" with a clock chip

shots.line: This film is built on physiology textbooks, diving manuals, clinical reviews and old laboratory reports.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: LIST card: Physiology textbooks / Diving manuals / Clinical reviews / Old laboratory reports (items reveal on words)
shots.footnote: Sources listed in the film description

shots.line: It is a calculation, not a prediction. And the unknowns are many.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "A calculation, not a prediction." sub "And the unknowns are many."

shots.line: Every number comes from a named source, or from arithmetic we show.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STAT-like plate "EVERY NUMBER: named source, or arithmetic we show"

shots.line: Where the sources disagree, we say so. Start with the number. Then the water. Then the fish. Then the liquid.
shots.scene: card: LIST numbered: The number / The water / The fish / The liquid, each on its word

shots.line: First, what a body needs.
shots.scene: torso: clay. Slow dolly down a seated clay figure from the head to the chest; TITLE "SETTING"

shots.line: At rest, an adult uses about two hundred and fifty millilitres of oxygen a minute.
shots.scene: torso: Torso cutaway, STAT plate "250 mL / min" with counting number
shots.footnote: Source: physiology course data · resting adult

shots.line: That is the figure in standard physiology teaching.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: "Standard physiology teaching" with textbook glyph, no outlet page faked

shots.line: One medical exam-prep page gets there from three and a half millilitres per kilogram, for a seventy-kilogram adult.
shots.scene: card: CALC card: 3.5 mL/kg/min x 70 kg = 245 mL/min, typed in on the words
shots.footnote: Source: medical exam-prep reference · arithmetic ours

shots.line: About two hundred and forty-five. Two hundred and fifty. Hold on to that. In air, it is easy to supply.
shots.scene: torso: Number 250 pulses; ring on lungs; pin "HOLD ON TO THAT"

shots.line: A litre of dry air is about twenty point nine percent oxygen, according to the United Nations food agency's fisheries manual.
shots.scene: bench: clay. Jar of air, camera push; TAG "20.9 % O2"

shots.line: That is about two hundred and nine millilitres in every litre.
shots.scene: bench: Jar fills with 209 clay dots, counter climbs to 209 mL per litre

shots.line: Resting breathing moves about five to eight litres of air a minute, according to the standard reference on minute ventilation. Call it six.
shots.scene: torso: Lungs with airflow arrows, chart-like counter "5-8 L/min"

shots.line: Six litres of air.
shots.scene: torso: Counter settles on "6 L/min"

shots.line: Two hundred and fifty millilitres of oxygen.
shots.scene: torso: Small glowing dot stream into blood vessel, label "250 mL O2"

shots.line: A comfortable, quiet job.
shots.scene: torso: Slow pull-out of calm breathing figure

shots.line: That is the deal the lungs were built around. Now change the fluid. Water holds oxygen too.
shots.scene: bench: clay. Jar of lake water next to the air jar; dip chapter "THE FIRST BREATH"

shots.line: Not much, says the sensor maker.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Not much."  source tag "Sensor manufacturer"
shots.footnote: Source: dissolved-oxygen sensor maker white paper

shots.line: A manufacturer of dissolved-oxygen sensors says air-saturated water at twenty-five
shots.scene: card: CALC card: air-saturated water, 25 C: 8.3 mg/L O2, typed on the words

shots.line: degrees holds about eight point three milligrams of oxygen per litre.
shots.scene: bench: clay. Dropper of mg-dots into water jar; label 8.3 mg

shots.line: Convert that, and it is about five point eight millilitres.
shots.scene: card: CALC arrow: 8.3 mg -> 5.8 mL per litre

shots.line: Our conversion, using a standard value for oxygen's density.
shots.scene: card: Footnote-style card: "our conversion" with density constant

shots.line: Two hundred and nine in air.
shots.scene: bench: Air jar glows: 209

shots.line: Five point eight in water. About thirty-six times less. Colder water holds more. Warm water holds less.
shots.scene: bench: Water jar 5.8; both jars side by side, bar ratio "36x"; small thermometer tag for cold/warm

shots.line: But the order of magnitude stays.
shots.scene: bench: Pull back, both jars on scale of 10 clay bars

shots.line: So how much water does she need?
shots.scene: torso: clay. Figure at lake edge, question tag "HOW MUCH WATER?"

shots.line: If her lungs took every last molecule, two hundred and fifty divided by five point eight is forty-three litres a minute.
shots.scene: bench: Counter 43 L fills a row of buckets as the numbers are spoken; CALC 250 / 5.8

shots.line: That is the floor. Physics will not let it go lower. But lungs do not take every molecule.
shots.scene: bench: Floor line drawn across buckets, tag "THE FLOOR"

shots.line: An arXiv paper on lung ventilation in mammals reports that exhaled air is sixteen to eighteen percent oxygen,
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: "arXiv paper, mammal ventilation" with 16-18 % O2 exhaled

shots.line: when the air going in is twenty-one. A drop of three to five points.
shots.scene: card: CHART bars: inhaled 21 %, exhaled 16-18 % with a 3-5 point bracket

shots.line: That is roughly a seventh to a quarter of what comes in. Our arithmetic. Take the generous end. A quarter.
shots.scene: card: Fraction bar: 1/7 to 1/4 highlighted, "generous end: a quarter"

shots.line: Two hundred and fifty, divided by five point eight, divided by a quarter.
shots.scene: bench: CALC card chain 250 / 5.8 / 0.25 builds term by term

shots.line: One hundred and seventy-two litres a minute.
shots.scene: bench: Bucket stack grows to 172, HERO "172 L / min"; flash
shots.footnote: Assumption: lungs take a quarter · arithmetic ours

shots.line: At the stingy end, it is more than three hundred. How much can a person breathe?
shots.scene: bench: Stingy end: bucket stack spills past frame, tag ">300 L"

shots.line: A physiology module at Monash University gives a mean maximum voluntary ventilation of about a hundred
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card "Monash University physiology module"

shots.line: and forty litres a minute for healthy young men.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: CHART bar 140 L/min (young men)

shots.line: Range, a hundred to a hundred and eighty. For women, about a hundred.
shots.scene: card: Range bracket 100-180 men; 100 women bar

shots.line: Seventy to a hundred and twenty.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Women range 70-120 whisker

shots.line: That is a short test, the module says, with the subject trying as hard as possible. Her resting need is higher than that. At rest.
shots.scene: card: CHART: bar 172 L vs bar 140 L, 172 higher; tag "AT REST"

shots.line: Then there is what water is.
shots.scene: bench: clay. Single bucket of water on a scale reading 1 kg; chapter "THE WEIGHT OF WATER"

shots.line: It is about eight hundred times denser than air.
shots.scene: bench: Air balloon vs water crate scale; tag "~800x DENSER"

shots.line: Course notes give a ratio of about eight hundred and thirty, a flashcard set says.
shots.scene: card: Statement "~830 (flashcard set)"; small source tag

shots.line: One litre of water weighs one kilogram.
shots.scene: bench: One litre bottle on scale: 1 kg

shots.line: A hundred and seventy-two litres a minute is a hundred and seventy-two kilograms. Through the throat. Every minute.
shots.scene: bench: Crate stack on scale climbs to 172 kg; tag on throat arrow

shots.line: While resting.
shots.scene: torso: Camera on throat, ring, tag "EVERY MINUTE"

shots.line: And the lung has a second problem.
shots.scene: torso: Lung drawn as branching tree, camera moves into the tree

shots.line: It breathes in and out through the same pipes.
shots.scene: torso: Arrows in and out through the same trunk

shots.line: A textbook puts the anatomical dead space at about a hundred and fifty millilitres, out of a resting breath of five hundred.
shots.scene: torso: Airway volume shaded: 150 mL of 500 mL; pin "DEAD SPACE"

shots.line: That is the volume of the airways themselves.
shots.scene: torso: Trunk and branches lit, 150 mL tag

shots.line: Whatever sits there at the end of an outbreath is stale. The next breath mixes with it. In air, that costs a little.
shots.scene: torso: Stale fluid in the branches turns grey; new fluid mixes

shots.line: The textbook says it leaves the oxygen pressure in the lung lower than in the air outside. In water, count it.
shots.scene: torso: Air-sac oxygen pressure lower than outside; small gauge

shots.line: Five hundred millilitres in.
shots.scene: torso: Bar: 500 mL in

shots.line: A hundred and fifty of it stale.
shots.scene: torso: 150 grey, 350 fresh split

shots.line: Three hundred and fifty reach the air sacs.
shots.scene: torso: 350 reaches sacs, ring

shots.line: To move a hundred and seventy-two litres of fresh water through them, that is nearly five hundred breaths a minute.
shots.scene: bench: CALC 172 / 0.35 = 491 breaths/min, ticker counting fast

shots.line: Or take the biggest breath she has.
shots.scene: torso: Big breath, lungs fully expanded

shots.line: Total lung capacity is about six litres, and the usual vital capacity is four point six to four point eight, depending on the source.
shots.scene: card: List: total capacity ~6 L; vital capacity 4.6-4.8 L (source differences noted)

shots.line: A full breath every time. Nearly forty a minute.
shots.scene: bench: Counter ~39 breaths/min

shots.line: Each one about four and a half kilograms of lake. Our arithmetic. Neither is a pace a person holds.
shots.scene: bench: Water-filled bucket 4.5 kg per breath; tag "NOT A PACE A PERSON HOLDS"

shots.line: No source we read says anyone has. All this is hypothetical. Here is what happens in the real world.
shots.scene: card: Dip. TITLE "WHAT HAPPENS TODAY" statement "This film is hypothetical"

shots.line: When someone inhales water, a clinical update on drowning describes two paths.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: clinical update on drowning

shots.line: In roughly ten to twenty percent of victims, the throat clamps shut. Laryngospasm.
shots.scene: torso: Throat cross-section closes: laryngospasm, ring

shots.line: The airway closes and the person asphyxiates, with little water reaching the lungs.
shots.scene: torso: Closed airway, no water reaches sacs

shots.line: Another source puts it lower, under ten to fifteen.
shots.scene: card: Range card: 10-20 % vs under 10-15 %

shots.line: In most, the throat relaxes and water goes in.
shots.scene: torso: Throat opens, small stream of water enters

shots.line: Victims typically aspirate about two to four millilitres per kilogram, according to the same reviews. A small volume.
shots.scene: card: STAT "2-4 mL / kg" with label aspirated

shots.line: But it does damage.
shots.scene: torso: Close on air sacs, tag "BUT IT DOES DAMAGE"

shots.line: The lungs line their air sacs with a thin film called surfactant. It keeps them open. Water disrupts it. The sacs collapse.
shots.scene: torso: Sacs with thin film (surfactant); water arrives; sacs collapse one by one

shots.line: Oxygen can no longer cross.
shots.scene: torso: Collapsed sacs, oxygen arrows blocked

shots.line: Older teaching said fresh water and salt water injure the lungs differently.
shots.scene: card: COMPARE: Fresh water
shots.footnote: Salt water, older teaching|Source: clinical review

shots.line: Current clinical sources say the practical difference is minor. The result is the same chain.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: COMPARE collapses to one line: "difference minor"

shots.line: Collapse, falling oxygen, rising carbon dioxide, and then the heart.
shots.scene: card: LIST chain: Collapse / Falling oxygen / Rising CO2 / The heart

shots.line: So our hero's lungs would need two things. A way to avoid the damage.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STATEMENT "Two things she would need"; item 1 on the words

shots.line: And a way to move far more water than any lung has moved. Remember the second. Fish do it. Every minute.
shots.scene: bench: Dip chapter "THE FISH". Bucket stack vs fish; "Remember the second"

shots.line: How? Two tricks. One.
shots.scene: gill: studio. Trout, two tricks list appears

shots.line: Their gills run blood and water in opposite directions.
shots.scene: gill: Gill arch cutaway; blood arrows left, water arrows right, opposite

shots.line: The most oxygen-rich blood meets the most oxygen-rich water. The least meets the least.
shots.scene: gill: Colour gradient strips: rich blood meets rich water

shots.line: Diffusion keeps working along the whole surface. How well does it work? Sources differ.
shots.scene: gill: Whole surface lit, tag "SOURCES DIFFER"

shots.line: A textbook says up to eighty-five percent of the oxygen in the water.
shots.scene: card: Bar 85 % (textbook)

shots.line: A school resource says about eighty.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Bar 80 % (school resource)

shots.line: The Natural History Museum in London says up to seventy.
shots.scene: card: Bar 70 % (Natural History Museum)

shots.line: An animal-physiology text says ninety or more is possible. Take eighty.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Bar 90 %+ (animal-physiology text); the 80 % bar highlighted: "TAKE EIGHTY"

shots.line: Two hundred and fifty, divided by five point eight, divided by point eight. About fifty-four litres a minute.
shots.scene: bench: CALC 250 / 5.8 / 0.8 = 54 L; bucket stack shrinks to 54

shots.line: Not one hundred and seventy-two. Two. The water flows one way.
shots.scene: gill: Trout, mouth intake arrow one-way; tag "ONE"

shots.line: It goes in the mouth, over the gills, out the side. No dead space. No stale pool in the airways.
shots.scene: gill: Water path mouth > gills > side opening; no dead end

shots.line: A physiology text says fish greatly reduce the energy cost of moving water by keeping that flow continuous and in one direction.
shots.scene: card: Source card: animal-physiology text on energy cost of flow

shots.line: A lung does the opposite. It is a dead-end sac.
shots.scene: torso: clay. Lung as dead-end sac, arrow in and out

shots.line: The same pipe in, the same pipe out.
shots.scene: torso: Same pipe, in and out

shots.line: So there is a first way to make her breathing work. Change her. Give her gills. Or something with gills' efficiency. A one-way flow.
shots.scene: torso: Split screen: lung

shots.line: A far better extraction. That is a different animal.
shots.scene: card: Statement "A different animal."

shots.line: Nothing in this film says it is impossible. It is not a lung anymore.
shots.scene: card: Statement "Not a lung anymore."

shots.line: Whether any human body could be rebuilt that way is not known.
shots.scene: card: Statement "Unknown: whether any human body could be rebuilt that way."

shots.line: Duke University, early nineteen-sixties. According to a Gizmodo history,
shots.scene: lab: clay. 1960s lab, sealed chamber, pressure gauge; card "DUKE UNIVERSITY · EARLY 1960s"

shots.line: Johannes Kylstra's team trained mice to breathe saline loaded with oxygen under a pressure of a hundred and sixty atmospheres.
shots.scene: lab: Mouse tank with saline jar, gauge climbs to 160 atm

shots.line: The mice died minutes later. Carbon dioxide had built up.
shots.scene: lab: Tank still; flash; text "CO2 built up"

shots.line: Another account says rodents and even dogs lasted up to about an hour. Accounts differ on the time. They agree on the cause.
shots.scene: card: COMPARE: Gizmodo (minutes) vs another account (up to about an hour); "ACCOUNTS DIFFER"

shots.line: The saline delivered enough oxygen.
shots.scene: lab: Oxygen dots reach the lung model

shots.line: It did not clear the carbon dioxide fast enough.
shots.scene: lab: CO2 dots pile up, not leaving

shots.line: The same fisheries manual says carbon dioxide is far more soluble in water than oxygen is.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: FAO manual on CO2 solubility

shots.line: Which is one reason gills shed it easily.
shots.scene: gill: CO2 leaving across a gill

shots.line: But a saline-filled lung is not a gill. Our reading:
shots.scene: torso: clay. Saline-filled lung vs gill; tag "OUR READING"
shots.footnote: Our reading · not tested in sources

shots.line: it is the same dead-end sac, filled with a liquid that barely moves. The sources do not test that.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "The sources do not test that."

shots.line: Mid-nineteen-sixties. Clark and Gollan. They switched the liquid. Not water. A perfluorocarbon.
shots.scene: lab: Mid-1960s lab, PFC flask, pale liquid; card "CLARK AND GOLLAN"

shots.line: A fluid that dissolves both gases.
shots.scene: lab: Two gas dots dissolving into the liquid

shots.line: Gizmodo says their mice breathed it at normal pressure.
shots.scene: lab: Mouse tank at normal pressure gauge 1 atm

shots.line: Rats stayed under for up to twenty hours. Cats, for weeks.
shots.scene: card: STAT row: rats up to 20 h, cats weeks

shots.line: An older encyclopedia mirror adds one detail that matters.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: older encyclopedia mirror

shots.line: The colder the liquid, the lower the animal's breathing rate.
shots.scene: lab: Thermometer falls, breathing rate counter falls

shots.line: That is the third way, and we will come back to it. First, the cost.
shots.scene: card: Statement "The third way. First, the cost."

shots.line: Perfluorocarbons are denser and more viscous than air.
shots.scene: lab: Liquid pouring thick vs air stream thin

shots.line: That raises the effort of breathing, according to Wikipedia's entry on liquid breathing. Mice are not people.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card Wikipedia; statement "Mice are not people."

shots.line: A mouse's lung is tiny. The distance is short. The volume is small.
shots.scene: lab: Tiny lung next to adult lung scale

shots.line: The sources here do not say whether the same method works at the size of an adult. That has not been shown.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Not shown at adult size."

shots.line: Look at what the cold did for the animals. It lowered their breathing rate. That is a fall in demand.
shots.scene: torso: clay. Dip chapter "THE THIRD WAY". Thermometer drop beside lungs, breathing slows

shots.line: Demand is the other half of the sum.
shots.scene: card: CALC card: demand x less -> litres x less

shots.line: If the body needed less oxygen, the two hundred and fifty would fall, and so would the litres.
shots.scene: torso: 250 shrinks, bucket stack shrinks

shots.line: For a human, the cold is not kind.
shots.scene: lake: day cold look. Swimmer shivers (small tremor), thermometer low

shots.line: A boating-safety guide says water draws heat from the body about twenty-five times faster than air at the same temperature.
shots.scene: card: STAT "25x faster heat loss"

shots.line: Other sources give four, twenty, and thirty-two. They all say faster.
shots.scene: card: Range chips 4 / 20 / 25 / 32

shots.line: The first danger is not hypothermia. It is cold shock. Sudden immersion makes people gasp.
shots.scene: lake: Swimmer gasps at the surface; tag "COLD SHOCK"

shots.line: Another guide says water inhaled in that gasp can cause unconsciousness within minutes. Hands and legs go numb.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: boating guide on gasping

shots.line: Within minutes, according to a New York state boating guide. Hypothermia comes later.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: New York State boating guide

shots.line: One expert average is about an hour, depending on temperature, clothing and body type.
shots.scene: card: CLOCK chip "~1 hour" with tag "ONE EXPERT AVERAGE"

shots.line: So the cold that helped the rats would not help her. Or not for long.
shots.scene: lake: Swimmer slows, camera pulls up

shots.line: Whether a human could be chilled safely enough to cut demand, while breathing liquid, has not been shown in the sources we found.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Unknown: safe chilling while breathing liquid"

shots.line: Philadelphia, nineteen eighty-nine. Three very premature babies.
shots.scene: ward: clay. Dip chapter "THE HUMAN CASE". Hospital corridor exterior; U.S. map pin Philadelphia

shots.line: Twenty-eight, twenty-four and twenty-three weeks of gestation.
shots.scene: card: STAT "28 · 24 · 23 weeks"; no infant imagery

shots.line: Doctors at Jefferson Medical College, led by Dr. J. S.
shots.scene: ward: Door sign "Jefferson Medical College", clay building

shots.line: Greenspan, tried perfluorocarbon in their lungs.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: Greenspan, J Pediatr 1990

shots.line: A review reports that their lung compliance improved.
shots.scene: card: STAT "compliance improved"

shots.line: The paper appeared in the Journal of Pediatrics in nineteen ninety. Note what it was. Partial liquid ventilation.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "PARTIAL liquid ventilation" with diagram: lungs filled, ventilator pushing gas

shots.line: The lungs were filled with the liquid, and a ventilator still pushed gas through it.
shots.scene: ward: Lung filled with liquid, ventilator gas line, schematic

shots.line: Not a baby breathing liquid alone.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Not liquid alone."

shots.line: Nineteen ninety-six.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: YEAR chip "1996"

shots.line: The LiquiVent study group reported thirteen infants with severe respiratory distress.
shots.scene: card: STAT "13 infants"

shots.line: In the New England Journal of Medicine, they say that within an hour of the treatment,
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: CHART bars start: oxygen tension, compliance; title "NEJM 1996 · 13 infants" held as the sentence begins

shots.line: arterial oxygen tension rose by a hundred and thirty-eight percent.
shots.scene: card: Bar 1 rises: arterial oxygen tension +138 %

shots.line: Compliance rose by sixty-one.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Bar 2 rises: compliance +61 %

shots.line: No adverse events were clearly attributable to it.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "No adverse events clearly attributable"

shots.line: That is the best result in this film. Then the footnote.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: HERO "The best result in this film"; then footnote chip

shots.line: Other clinical trials, a review notes, failed to show that partial liquid ventilation reduced illness in acute respiratory failure.
shots.scene: card: LIST footnote: other trials failed to show reduced illness in acute respiratory failure

shots.line: It is not a lake, and it is not an adult swimmer.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: COMPARE: Ward

shots.line: A premature lung is not a healthy one, and a controlled ward is not open water.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Not a healthy lung. Not open water."

shots.line: Whether a healthy adult could breathe liquid for hours has not been established. Now take her down.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STATEMENT "Not established: a healthy adult, for hours." then dip
shots.footnote: Not established in the sources read

shots.line: Pressure rises about one atmosphere for every ten metres of seawater.
shots.scene: depth: clay. Dip chapter "DOWN". Water column, clay mannequin at 0 m, depth gauge, slow descent

shots.line: That figure is consistent across diving sources.
shots.scene: depth: Pressure labels at 10, 20, 30 m appear as the gauge passes them

shots.line: At thirty metres, four atmospheres in total. Our sum.
shots.scene: depth: Mannequin at 30 m; STAT "4 atm total"

shots.line: Divers on air meet two problems there. One is the gas itself.
shots.scene: depth: Air-diver sketch with two icons: narcosis and bends; tag "ON AIR"

shots.line: A training article says the effects of inert-gas narcosis are second only to oxygen toxicity in hazard for an air diver.
shots.scene: card: SOURCE card: training article on inert-gas narcosis

shots.line: The other is the bends.
shots.scene: depth: Camera on diver's chest; tag "THE BENDS"

shots.line: The extra pressure drives more nitrogen into the blood.
shots.scene: depth: Nitrogen dots drift into a blood vessel

shots.line: Come up too fast and it comes out as bubbles. Joint pain.
shots.scene: depth: Fast ascent: dots become bubbles, joint ring

shots.line: In severe cases, stroke or paralysis.
shots.scene: card: LIST: Joint pain / Stroke / Paralysis (severe cases)

shots.line: The standard advice is an ascent of about ten metres a minute or slower. Oxygen is the third. Dive rules cap its pressure.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STAT "~10 m / min" ascent; tag "ABOUT, OR SLOWER"; then oxygen icon

shots.line: The U.S.
shots.scene: card: Title card building: "U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY"

shots.line: Environmental Protection Agency's regional dive plan says nitrox diving is generally limited to one point four atmospheres.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STAT "1.4 ATA nitrox limit"

shots.line: A quoted NOAA manual says one point six. Air is twenty-one percent oxygen. Multiply by the pressure.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "A quoted NOAA manual: 1.6" and CALC chip "21 % x pressure"
shots.footnote: Source: forum quote of NOAA manual · secondary

shots.line: About sixty metres on air, and the limit is reached.
shots.scene: depth: Gauge arrow stops near 60 m, tag "LIMIT ON AIR"

shots.line: Our arithmetic, at four atmospheres per thirty. But she is not breathing air.
shots.scene: depth: Mannequin without tank, water in the lungs, tags "OUR ARITHMETIC" and "NOT AIR"

shots.line: What would pressure do to someone breathing water?
shots.scene: depth: Question tag above mannequin: "PRESSURE?"

shots.line: Would nitrogen dissolve into her blood? Would it bubble on the way up?
shots.scene: depth: Nitrogen tag, bubble tag, two question marks

shots.line: That has not been published, as far as we could find. It is unclear what the answer would be.
shots.scene: card: STATEMENT "Not published, as far as we could find."

shots.line: Here is where it stands on Monday, the twenty-sixth of October, twenty twenty-six. What is known.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Dip. TITLE "WHERE IT STANDS", date chip "Monday 26 October 2026"; wall begins "KNOWN"

shots.line: Water holds about thirty-six times less oxygen than air.
shots.scene: card: STAT "36x less oxygen in water"

shots.line: A resting adult needs about two hundred and fifty millilitres a minute.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STAT "250 mL / min"

shots.line: Even with generous extraction, that is a hundred and seventy-two litres of water a minute, and nearly five hundred breaths.
shots.scene: card: STAT "172 L / min · ~500 breaths / min"
shots.footnote: Arithmetic ours · assumption: a quarter extracted

shots.line: Fish do it with one-way flow and gills, at about fifty-four. Mice and rats have breathed liquid.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: STAT "54 L / min · fish" then LIST: mice and rats breathed liquid

shots.line: Premature infants have had partial liquid ventilation. What is not known.
shots.scene: card: LIST: Premature infants: partial liquid ventilation; wall flips to "NOT KNOWN"

shots.line: How a healthy adult would fare breathing liquid for hours.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Item 1 "How a healthy adult would fare, for hours"

shots.line: How much a human lung could really extract.
shots.scene: card: Item 2 "How much a human lung could extract"

shots.line: What pressure would do to someone breathing water. Where the answers sit. In primary papers we did not read.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: Item 3 "What pressure does to a water breather"; then "WHERE THE ANSWERS SIT"

shots.line: The Kylstra and Clark papers. The Greenspan paper. The LiquiVent trial. Textbooks on gill physiology.
shots.scene: card: LIST of primary papers to read: Kylstra, Clark and Gollan, Greenspan, the LiquiVent trial; textbooks

shots.line: Naval diving research. This is a calculation. Not a finding. Two metres under a lake.
shots.scene: bench: 3D clay slab/bar version of the card, slow push; overlay keeps the same numbers and words. Card spec: LIST ends "Naval diving research"; STATEMENT "A calculation. Not a finding."

shots.line: A person, breathing.
shots.scene: lake: dusk. Same framing as shot one: still water, pier; camera sinks; text "A person, breathing."

shots.line: Six litres a minute of air.
shots.scene: lake: Swimmer breathing; HERO chip "6 L / min of air"

shots.line: A hundred and seventy-two of water. The lungs were built for the first.
shots.scene: lake: Same frame, HERO chip "172 L / min of water"; slow pull-out to the empty pier at dusk; fade
